title: な versus の, and なる / たる adjectives
summary: Japanese is noun-centered: な-adjectives, の-adjectives and する-verbs are all nouns. な is the copula before a noun, の links a noun to a noun, and なる / たる are old-style forms.

blocks.text: The course models a sentence as a **train**: three kinds of **engines** (verbs, い-adjectives, and noun + だ) pull noun **carriages** marked by particles. So everything that is not a verb or an い-adjective is a noun, even words dictionaries file under "adjective".
A word like 綺麗 is a **noun** that is used as a description. The copula だ becomes **な** before a noun, so だ and な are the same word.
Some such words also work as ordinary nouns and take particles: 元気 (healthy) can be 元気な子供, but also 元気を出して. Only nouns take case particles like を, so that proves it.
Any noun can describe another with **の**.

blocks.jp: 魔法の帽子をかぶった。
blocks.en: I put on a magic hat.

blocks.text: Some words take either な or の, and the feel changes:

rows: a country that is itself strange

blocks.text: A noun + **する** becomes a verb: 勉強 + する = 勉強する. It is the one big exception where an imported noun really acts as a verb. Because 勉強 is a noun, it can also take を.

blocks.jp: 毎日日本語を勉強する。

blocks.text: Two nouns can simply sit side by side: 本棚 (bookshelf), 日本語 (the Japanese language). In longer chains each noun describes the one after it. A word written only in kanji, with no okurigana, is almost always a noun.

blocks.en: There are books on the bookshelf.

blocks.text: なる and たる: the literary forms
Words like 華麗なる探偵 or 堂々たる態度 sound old-fashioned and grand. They are nouns too, in an old-style attributive form, and work like "magnificent" in a title.

blocks.jp: 華麗なる探偵が現れた。

blocks.en: He spoke with a dignified manner.

items: **Noun + な + noun**: an adjectival noun described by the copula.
**Noun + の + noun**: any noun modifies another.
**なる / たる**: grand, literary descriptive forms.
